analysis.one_liner: Requires oil and gas drillers on federal lands to replace damaged water supplies, compensate surface owners, and reclaim and bond disturbed land.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in May 2005 and died there when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted oil and gas drilling — especially coalbed methane — on western lands where the federal government owns the minerals but private owners hold the surface. It would have required drillers to replace water supplies their operations contaminated or depleted, submit water management plans with lease applications, get state pollution permits for extracted water, reach a compensation agreement with (or arbitrate with) surface owners before drilling, meet reclamation standards, and post reclamation bonds. It also set up a federal program to clean up abandoned wells and aid states and tribes with their own abandoned-well problems.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, ranchers, and other surface owners in western states whose land sits atop federally owned oil and gas. They would gain advance notice of lease sales, a say in drilling plans, compensation for crop, livestock, and property damage, and restoration of their land after drilling. Rural water users would gain replacement of supplies contaminated or cut off by drilling, and taxpayers would gain a funded program to plug abandoned wells leaking on federal and adjacent lands.

how_it_helps.text: Operators would have to replace water supplies for domestic, agricultural, or other users whose water was contaminated, diminished, or interrupted by drilling, and file a water management plan with each lease application.

Drillers could not begin work on split-estate lands without a signed surface-use agreement — covering limited surface use, reclamation, and compensation for damages like lost crops and livestock — unless they made a good-faith attempt, went through operator-paid arbitration, or met bonding and plan requirements set by the Secretary of the Interior.
Operators would have to restore affected land to a condition capable of supporting its prior uses and post reclamation bonds sufficient to cover the cost if the government had to do the work instead.

The Interior Department would run a remediation program for abandoned wells on federal lands and wells that tapped federally owned minerals, with $5 million per year authorized, plus technical assistance programs for states and Indian tribes.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers — including coalbed methane operators — drilling on or near federal mineral leases. They would bear the cost of replacing damaged water, negotiating and paying for surface-use agreements and arbitration, posting reclamation and damage bonds, and cleaning up wells. The public treasury would fund the abandoned-well remediation and assistance programs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs — water replacement, arbitration, bonds, reclamation — would fall on operators and could make some marginal drilling projects uneconomical, and the bill's own findings acknowledge domestic oil and gas (including coalbed methane) as part of the nation's energy supply; opponents could argue the requirements would curb production.

The bill was not airtight: the Secretary could still authorize drilling without any surface-owner agreement if the operator made a good-faith attempt to negotiate, submitted an adequate plan, and posted a bond, so surface owners could still end up with a drilling operation on their land over their objection.

The abandoned-well cleanup would be funded by taxpayers ($5 million a year for federal fiscal years 2006 through 2007 and 2008 programs), even though the bill also directs the Secretary to recover costs from responsible parties where possible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose real, targeted costs on drillers in exchange for protecting western water, farmland, and private property rights from damage they currently cause without a federal consent or bonding framework. Its weaknesses are that the no-agreement loophole lets drilling proceed over a surface owner's objection with only a bond as protection, and that it adds federal compliance layers on an energy-producing industry. On balance it shifts costs from injured landowners and water users to the companies causing the damage, at some risk to drilling economics.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, parceled out to subcommittees, and never moved again — no markup, no floor vote, no Senate action — before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Representative Mark Udall of Colorado introduced the bill on May 3, 2005, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure for the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.

In the following two weeks it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee (May 4) and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee (May 13), and executive comment was requested from Interior.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee at the end of the 109th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators, especially coalbed methane producers on split-estate western lands, avoided new water-replacement, surface-owner-consent, reclamation, and bonding requirements; surface owners and water users got no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal lands

for.name: Rep. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor; it was his bill alone.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee took no markup or vote; the bill never left the committee.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee took no markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, which is the only available signal of support.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers, especially coalbed methane operators
industries.note: The bill would have imposed water-replacement duties, surface-use agreements or arbitration with landowners, reclamation standards, and reclamation and damage bonds on federal-lease drilling. Its costs were the public's protections, so the industry's interest ran against the surface owners and water users the bill served.

industries.industry: Western farmers and ranchers (split-estate surface owners)
industries.note: Millions of acres of western surface land is privately owned while the federal government kept the oil and gas underneath; current law requires surface-owner consent for coal but not for oil and gas, which the bill would have changed. Their gains — notice, compensation, reclamation, water replacement — are the same gains ordinary water users and rural communities would have gotten.

industries.industry: Taxpayers and state and tribal governments
industries.note: The bill created a federal program to remediate abandoned wells on federal lands and tapped federally owned minerals, plus technical assistance for states and tribes dealing with abandoned wells on their lands, with modest appropriations authorized.
